item.title: REVIEW: Headed to Puerto Rico? These Beaches Belong on Your Bucket List
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
My father grew up on Puerto Rico's west coast, where beach days began with a barefoot walk to the sand around the neighborhoods of Isabela or Aguadilla and often ended wherever the waves happened to be breaking next. I grew up on stories of salty hair, sun-warmed sand, and long, glittering afternoons in the water. Eventually, I started following in his footsteps, exploring the island’s beaches for myself and discovering just how many different shades of paradise fit along its 300 miles of coastline. There are the rollicking Atlantic surf breaks at Jobos and Middles, the impossibly blue waters and colorful fishing boats of Crash Boat, the mangrove-fringed coastline around La Parguera, and the powdery white sands of Culebra's Flamenco Beach. Some days call for a boat ride out to Culebrita’s secluded Tortuga Beach; others are better spent under the palms in Luquillo, with a plate of fresh seafood and a cold Medalla from the nearby kiosks. The island is filled with beaches, all with a slightly different personality. Whether your plan is to wake up early and arrive with a surfboard, head out on a boat ride, snorkel, or lounge on the sand with absolutely no plans at all, I've got a rec for you. From well-loved surf towns to far-flung island hideaways, these are the best beaches in Puerto Rico worth building a trip around—plus, where to stay when you get there. item.title: IDEA: Why You Should Pack Your Hiking Boots on a Trip to St. Croix
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The smell hit me out of nowhere: an uncanny whiff of sweaty socks. I instinctively glanced around for another hiker. My guide, local naturalist Olasee Davis, laughed and pointed to a thick brown seed pod lying on the trail. It had fallen from a West Indian locust, more commonly known as a stinking toe tree. The culprit loomed farther down the trail, its massive limbs weaving a vaulted canopy overhead. “It tastes better than it smells,” Olasee said, picking up the pod and cracking it open on a rock to reveal the powdery pulp inside. I watched him take a bite but decided to pass. I suspected stinking toe fruit was an acquired taste, and with only a few days remaining on my trip to St. Croix, I'd save the acquiring for a future visit. As we continued along, Olasee introduced me to other tropical evergreens, including the soursop, laden with spiky fruit, and the red manjack, much shorter and shrubbier, with brownish-red berries. Around the next bend he pointed out nonnative fruit trees: papaya from South America and mango from India. But he hadn't brought me here just for the botany. He'd brought me to understand why this forest matters. As an ecologist, historian, and assistant professor at the University of the Virgin Islands, Olasee helped lead the effort to establish Maroon Sanctuary Territorial Park in 2025. Encompassing 2,469 acres in the northwest corner of St. Croix, the park protects part of Maroon Country, the island's steep, forested interior where people who had escaped slavery found refuge during the 1700s and early 1800s. The new park also safeguards former sugar plantations and mill sites, which have been slowly returning to nature since Denmark ended slavery in the Danish West Indies (present-day US Virgin Islands) in 1848. By that time more than 100,000 enslaved Africans had passed through the port of Christiansted on St. Croix, the largest of the islands, to be sold to plantation owners in the Danish Caribbean sugar economy. Olasee and I were following an old plantation trail through one such former estate when he suddenly stopped and then scrambled up a steep embankment into the trees. I followed, brushing aside slender branches. Hidden beneath the understory, almost swallowed by spider lilies, was a burial ground. Most graves were marked with conch shells. Some were covered by low, weathered concrete slabs. One was marked by a headstone, its inscription softened by decades of moisture and lichen. The hidden cemetery wasn't an isolated discovery. For more than 40 years, Olasee has bushwhacked his way through Maroon Country to search for burial grounds and other traces of those who escaped slavery, documenting sites that would otherwise disappear beneath the forest. Now that it's been conserved as a territorial park, that work can continue in a more systematic, permanent way. Or as Olasee put it, “I could die in peace now.” Travelers have traditionally come to the USVI for beach vacations and sailing charters; now Maroon Sanctuary is opening up another side to the islands. The park's founders are also building out an official trail network. The roughly 10 miles of trail that I explored with Olasee were a patchwork of former estate roads, plantation footpaths, and forgotten forest routes that he'd pieced together over decades. Soon these trails will be easier to navigate without needing someone like Olasee to lead the way. The next morning I met Kristina “Kitty” Edwards, director of the US Virgin Islands Division of Territorial Parks & Protected Areas, at a trailhead on the slopes of 1,165-foot Mount Eagle, the island's highest peak. We were about to hike the first official segment of the trail, a three-mile loop designed for hiking and mountain biking, which opened this past May. When completed, the trail system will wend 30 miles through the forested backcountry. As excited as Kitty was to show off the new path, a first of its kind on the island, she wasn't in a hurry. “I'm a meanderer,” she said with a shrug and a smile. In the shirt-soaking heat of the tropics, I was grateful to take it slow. We ascended amid white-winged butterflies and yellow-breasted bananaquits. After an hour we reached the stone remnants of the old watchtower that marked the summit. A spur trail led us to an overlook where we paused to take in the 270-degree view, bookended by emerald peaks to our right and the inviting turquoise waters of Cane Bay to our left. It occurred to me that Maroon Sanctuary wasn't just about the land. The park's protected boundary extends all the way to the sea, helping shield Cane Bay's coral reefs and the nearby Annaly Bay tide pools from pollution and sediment. I spent the next day reveling in those crystal waters. At Sweet Bottom Dive Center, I rented a mask and fins, and went snorkeling among the parrotfish, angelfish, and wrasse that inhabit the shallow reef just offshore. After watching a sea turtle munch on seagrass, I flipped over onto my back. Above the beach the densely forested peaks of Maroon Country rose in layers, a physical reminder of the many lives and histories held within. The Waves at Cane Bay, an 11-room boutique hotel built into the rocky shoreline overlooking the bay, was reimagined in 2021 as a stylish oceanfront retreat with private patios, two bars, and the sustainable seafood restaurant Ama. The hotel is a four-minute walk to the beach at Cane Bay and a nine-minute drive to the new Mount Eagle trailhead. Located directly across the road from Cane Bay, the Landing Beach Bar serves up Caribbean specialties like jerk chicken and fried plantains in a fun, convivial setting. Leatherback Brewing Company is St. Croix's first craft brewery and an unofficial headquarters for the island's mountain-biking community, complete with a full-service bike shop inside.

item.title: All the 2026 National Eater Award Winners, Mapped
item.description:
Source: Eater
The 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, now in their 17th year, capture the breadth of dining in the U.S., celebrating the best new restaurants across the country. This year’s awards recognize not only restaurants, but also the best in bakeries, pioneering chefs, and standout dishes, as well as the Best New Bars as designated by Eater’s sister publication, Punch. Each winner is a testament to the idea that dining out is still worth the effort and cost it can command — as long as you know where to look. All the 2026 National Eater Award Winners, Mapped The best restaurants, bakeries, chefs, dishes, and bars across the country Eater is partnering with select Eater Award winners to offer special dining perks now through January 31, 2027. To access these exclusive perks, create an Eater account or download and create an account on the Eater app for iOS. (Terms apply) One of Eater’s 2026 Best New Bakeries, the Pastry Project, offers training to people facing barriers to employment in Pioneer Square. Head to the walk-up window for innovative items that rotate weekly — feather-light peanut butter and raspberry jelly cake, elephant ear-esque cardamom croissants, and apple pie cream puffs topped with cider meringue, to name a few. Show up Thursday through Saturday morning, but be prepared for a line. In the summer, the spot doubles as a soft-serve ice cream stand. Occupying the former SE Division home of a different well-known Northern Thai-influenced restaurant, OK Chicken & Khao Soi was perhaps Portland’s biggest opening of the year. Akkapong “Earl” Ninsom (Yaowarat, Langbaan, and PaaDee, to name a few) and Eric Nelson (Expatriate, Eem, Phuket Cafe) — two of Portland’s most well-respected culinary talents — bring to life Chiang Mai-style dining in a space that feels simultaneously intimate and energetic, in the spirit of a really good dinner party. Named a 2026 Best New Restaurant in the U.S. winner, this spot puts emphasis on its namesake dishes, but don’t ignore the other items on the menu. Slushies and shakes cut the heat of Thai chiles, and richly seasoned and marinated dishes like gai yang chicken legs or sai ouia herbal sausages sing alongside bright basil, crisp cucumbers, and savory side sauces. Reservations are accepted. Cassis, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, is big in every sense. The nearly 200-seat dining room of the Milwaukee restaurant is an immaculately designed jewel box of gleaming tile, cozy banquettes, and antique mirrors, and even on a Wednesday night, it’s packed and roaring, with a towering, glowing bar at the center of the action. The latest project from Kyle and Meghan Knall, the couple behind nearby acclaimed bistro Birch, channels the conviviality and polish of an old-world French brasserie while remaining distinctly Midwestern in spirit. It’s an all-day restaurant with both heart and panache. — Hilary Pollack Tucked behind Lonesome Rose, a casual Tex-Mex restaurant in Chicago, a short stairway leads to an unassuming door. There’s no sign, but there is a logo — a snake entwined around a bottle — and the faint sounds of a salsa soundtrack playing Puerto Rican music. This is how you know you’re at Culebra, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars. With cocktails that tap Malta India (a nonalcoholic malt beverage), tamarind, and culantro, this bar is an homage to Puerto Rican flavors and the Latinx influences of the surrounding neighborhood, Logan Square. Owner Diego Garcia-Gonzalez was born and raised there, and worked his way up through Chicago’s bar industry, beginning in 2013 at age 15, then began visiting Puerto Rico in 2024 to do guest bartending shifts. Behind the bar, you’ll spy a menu of $12 daily Daiquiris, made with a different rum blend each day. Take Friday’s offering: It features Uruapan Charanda, Chairman’s 1931 and Cachaça Amburana, brought perfectly into balance for a richly layered drink. — Amy Cavanaugh Perk: Eater members receive a free order of tostones with the purchase of any two Cocteles Originales through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply) When Creepies opened in mid-2025, the chatter about this Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant centered on its name. Now, those in the know focus on the food that balances French culinary know-how with a Midwestern sensibility to create a restaurant that’s charming in so many ways. Equal parts bistro and chic diner, Creepies is the brainchild of David and Anna Posey — the husband-and-wife chefs behind next-door Elske, stellar in its own right — and chef Tayler Ploshehanski. Start with warm Brie gougères as you linger over the wine list full of intriguing offerings, before moving on to heartier dishes like steamed mussels with fennel, roasted chicken in a liver and wine sauce, and Parisian gnocchi. Save room for one of Anna’s desserts, including a rotating soft-serve sundae. After three years as Noah Sandoval’s chef de cuisine at two-Michelin-starred Oriole, Larry Feldmeier partnered with the James Beard Award-winner to open All Well in April. Located inside the former La Sardine space, the West Loop restaurant’s menu features a modern American five-course tasting menu ($145) and a la carte bar fare with Japanese and French inflections. Plates like candied beets with sake lees, sea buckthorn, and endive, and sablefish with savoy cabbage, amazake, and genmai, and sweet and briny Hokkaido scallops with celtuce, Virginia ham XO sauce, and coriander, are matched by cocktails like the dirty daiquiri — a martini-adjacent riff featuring white rum, green olive, lime, and Calvados brandy. The puffed grain toast on the tasting menu at All Well is an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year. This Hingetown newcomer from James Beard-recognized chef Vinnie Cimino, also behind Cleveland critical darling Cordelina, is devoted to ancestral European fare. Rosy’s constantly changing menu is posted on a wooden board above the counter seating. Seasonal vegetables are a major focus, and the majority of the menu is fueled by live-fire cooking. The pickled walleye cheeks, a sometimes special, are an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year; consider starting an order with the restaurant’s bread and spreads variety, and make sure one of their pork sausage dishes is in the mix. Ahris Kim, one of the forces behind acclaimed NYC restaurants like Atomix and Atoboy, opened her own restaurant in June in Greenwich Village, under parent company Na:Eun Hospitality. Somssi, a 2026 Eater Best New Restaurant, is a neo-bistro with an a la carte menu full of dishes featuring Korean, European, and other Asian touches; see dishes like grilled ox tongue with romesco sauce and the carby Potato Potato Potato. A new cocktail bar devoted to all things rum opened in Williamsburg in the former Gertie space. Echo Lake, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, offers $12 daily daiquiris and a lager/rum shot combo cutely called Tiny and a Tot, plus seafood-centric plates like oysters with tepache mignonette and green coconut curry chowder. The new bar comes from beverage power-couple Chloe Frechette (the former executive editor at Eater sibling site Punch) and Paul McGee, who cut his teeth at Chicago’s now-closed tropical bar Lost Lake. The duo is also featuring their own collection of liquid loot within the intimate basement rum bar, Undercurrent. Perk: Eater members get a free side of soft serve with the purchase of any full-price cocktail through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply) With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān, one of Eater’s 2026 Best New Bakeries, gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights. Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury Perk: Eater members get a free Afghan chai with the purchase of any pastry through January 31, 2027. Terms apply. Sunday is a very good night to be at Titusz, a 2026 Eater Best New Restaurant. That’s Schnitzel Sonntag — when the Pittsburgh restaurant, clad in warm wood and gem-toned ceramic tile, offers an irresistible special at an even more irresistible price: a 4-ounce veal cutlet, breaded and fried in lard, for $13. Chef and owner Csilla Thackray honed her craft in some of the city’s top restaurant kitchens. Thackray’s husband, Sean Rosenkrans — another veteran of Pittsburgh’s restaurant and bar scene — has built a stunning list of wines from Central Europe, as well as cocktails fluent in that idiom. Don’t miss the sour cherry soup and the kaspressknödel (cheese dumpling) in charred leek and sauerkraut broth. — Beth Kracklauer From the team behind Mawn, one of the city’s most beloved and lauded restaurants, comes sibling Sao. Like Mawn, it’s influenced by Southeast Asian flavors, but Sao is more focused on seafood and has a liquor license. That means you can have a well-made martini or glass of wine with your scallops and crab curry from James Beard Award-winning chef Phila Lorn, who is also an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year. Assuming new ownership of beloved, old restaurants can be a risk, but South Philly local Joey Baldino has the formula down: Keep the trappings, dial in the food. After taking over his family’s private Palizzi Social Club and retaining its members-only allure, Baldino bought Bomb Bomb Bar, which first opened in 1951, and reopened it last year. In the front room of this Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, locals analyze Eagles games, and you might hear children playing in the street. In the back dining room, the procession of seafood, priced at $65 per person, feels like a steal in this era of rising prices. The meat for the lobster Française has been removed from its shell, battered and fried, placed on a buttery sauce, and then crowned with its shell once more. The crispy calamari gets enlivened with twangy cherry peppers. But it’s the overall dining experience that’s unbeatable: The restaurant hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but as the Beach Boys play and you sip a pepperoncini martini while watching your server pour hot fudge onto a sundae, you remember (perhaps while still wearing a bib) that complete novelty isn’t always necessary. — Bettina Makalintal One of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, Peach Crease Club’s cocktail menu reads like a list of favorite foods from around the world: Buko Salad from the Philippines, Borscht from Ukraine, Guayaba y Queso from Latin America. But the dishes-turned-drinks are just one half of Peach Crease Club’s identity. The other is music, and the two complement each other like dinner and a show. Alex Jump, co-owner of the bar (and one of Punch’s Best New Bartenders in 2019), cooked in Denver kitchens like ChoLon before moving behind the stick, and she’s been building culinary-focused cocktails since her Death & Co. Denver days. It’s not a trend she and her husband, co-owner and fellow industry vet Stuart Jensen, are chasing, Jump says; it’s just how they like to drink. Order such cocktails as the Gibson riff the Fattoush and the Guayaba y Queso; the Kik Alicha, named for Ethiopia’s turmeric split pea stew, sits under split-pea foam with a berbere garnish. — Nickolaus Hines McLain Hedges and Mary Allison Wright of Yacht Club fame run Rougarou, a cozy-cool tribute to Southern cuisine in Five Points, which guarantees that the beverage program is a winner: Cocktails like the Sorghum Daiquiri and the Bananas Foster Julep hit the spot, and the wine selection is small but smart. What’s surprising is the food at this 2026 Best New Restaurant, which is both thoughtful and soulful, prepared by Wright’s brother, exec chef John David Wright. Creative dishes like West Indies crab salad with butter crackers, hot-and-sour catfish, fairytale eggplant with ancho chile peanut butter and ricotta salata, and rice pudding with pumpkin-white chocolate ganache and pecan praline bring something completely new to the Denver table. Akoya Omakase, a 2026 Best New Restaurant, is the latest project from chef Peter Hoang. The vibe here is relaxed elegance, with affable chefs at the counter showcasing pristine fish in a way that highlights its best qualities, whether pairing golden threadfin bream with umami-laden shiso salt, or smoky juvenile king mackerel with pineapple chutney. Dishes that sound like they might not work on paper sing, like a hirame sashimi accented with kelp salt and both white truffle oil and black truffle pate. Akoya lacks the self-seriousness that some omakases can fall prey to, with chefs explaining dishes in straightforward language, and diners chatting enthusiastically with each other at the counter and even across tables in the small dining room. D.C. hospitality veterans Jon Sybert and Jill Tyler took a risk when they converted Adams Morgan’s Michelin-starred favorite Tail Up Goat into Rye Bunny, a restaurant that straddles the line between upscale and casual. Rye Bunny, one of Eater’s 2026 Best New Restaurants, encompasses the simple joy of a neighborhood restaurant that’s an equally excellent destination for a weekday date night or a special occasion, and it represents a larger shift in our dining landscape that might save these mid-price-range restaurants as margins get thinner. Be sure to order the Aleppo honey-covered fried chicken, as well as the anchovy and quince jam toasts. — Emily Venezky Perk: Eater members get a free pour of dessert wine with purchase of dessert; up to two pours per dessert through January 31, 2027. (21+ | Terms apply) Maru San, a counter spot for Nikkei-style cuisine from decorated Peruvian chef Carlos Delgado, an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year, debuted on Friday, February 20. Delgado, who also runs Shaw’s one-Michelin-starred tasting room Causa and won the 2025 James Beard Award for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic, adds a sleek, 25-seat counter in Eastern Market for hand rolls and sets, a la carte dishes, and a selection of Japanese beers, sake, and nonalcoholic offerings like a chicha morada and matcha lemonade. During a nightly experience, available for four guests at a time, the Lima-born chef puts a fine dining spin on the fusion food he’s already familiar with. Nikkei cuisine is a specialty at José Andrés’s China Chilcano — the Penn Quarter ceviche spot where Delgado was previously the longtime executive chef. Bar Roza, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, can be found down a quiet alleyway that runs through Nashville’s oldest shopping corridor, the Arcade. There, restaurateur Julia Jaksic (who also runs Cafe Roze and Roze Pony) has turned a former storage room into a rose-tinted oasis of pink marble where partner and beverage director Owen Gibler’s cocktails take center stage. Venture into the Polythermal Arcade, a section of the menu where each drink is served two ways, cold and hot. Order the Jet Pilot, a riff on the tiki classic with rums swizzled with grapefruit, lime, and cinnamon over crushed ice, then have it again as the Radio Flyer, topped with steamed almond milk. — Ellen Fort San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery, one of Eater’s 2026 Best New Bakeries, steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials). Be sure to order the lychee bowtie croissant, black sesame and yuzu cookie, and savory croissants. — Dianne de Guzman Perk: Eater members get a free off-menu item or mini croissant with the purchase of any pastry through January 31, 2027. Terms apply. In an unmarked space in San Francisco’s Nob Hill, chef Patrick Gabon and partner Celine Wuu quietly rewrote the playbook on fine dining with Restaurant Naides, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant. Filipino food has not historically held a footing in the Bay Area’s higher-end echelons, but Naides’s dishes make a powerful claim that the cuisine deserves its place there. Be sure to order Gabon’s takes on classic dishes like bagoong, sinigang, and lumpia; the nonalcoholic beverage pairing is also worth exploring. — Dianne de Guzman San Francisco first came to know chefs Laura and Sayat Ozyilmaz through their pop-up Istanbul Modern, and later through their breakthrough Presidio restaurant Dalida. The duo’s success is grounded in their take on Eastern Mediterranean food, which they made a conscious decision to champion 10 years ago. Fast-forward to 2026, and now Laura Ozyilmaz, an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year, is taking on a personal project of her own, with Sayat by her side, placing foods from Mexico’s Guerrero and Sinaloa center stage at Maria Isabel. It’s a refreshing menu that combines both Mexican and local ingredients through the lens of the Ozyilmazes’ cooking backgrounds. Order such dishes as the ceviche Acapulqueño, duck carnitas enmoladas, and artichoke tetela. — Dianne de Guzman Perk: Eater members get a free seasonal tepache with the purchase of a tasting menu through January 31, 2027. Terms apply. Philip Krajeck, the chef behind Rolf and Daughters and Folk, has been building his empire of hip, cozy restaurants since 2012, and his latest is no exception. Junior, tucked into what was once a Dickerson Pike Piggly Wiggly grocery store, is one of Nashville’s hottest new dining rooms. The wine list is a standout, curated by Billy Smith (formerly of award-winning natural wine bar the Four Horsemen, in Brooklyn) and featuring hard-to-find producers and dusty bottles straight from the cellar. Chef Brian Mejia (Rolf and Daughters) is leading the kitchen, showcasing dishes with elegant French techniques and Southern charm, like collard green barbajuan with burnt lemon, blue crab raviolo with herbs and blossoms, and chicory root ice cream with espresso caramel. The cantaloupe verjus terrine on the tasting menu is an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year. Find white tablecloths, red leather banquettes, a shiny, red-lacquered wine station, and an open kitchen with a roaring wood-fired stove here. Kwame Onwuachi’s arrival in Las Vegas has been a spectacle. Fire dancers, showgirls, a performance from Busta Rhymes, and a poolside drone show helped kick off the highly anticipated opening of Maroon, his Caribbean steakhouse inside Sahara Las Vegas. Maroon is the first West Coast restaurant from the James Beard Foundation Award–winning chef following his acclaimed Tatiana in New York City and Dōgon in Washington, D.C. At Maroon, a 2026 Best New Restaurant, steaks are rum-aged, the fried rice has chunks of oxtail and curry-spiced shrimp, and a jerk pit in the middle of the restaurant turns out jerk chicken, tender lamb chops, and pork tomahawks. Other signatures include wood-fired lobster, crawfish mashed potatoes, and creamed coconut collards. The only thing about Oklahoma City that feels even vaguely reminiscent of the Caribbean is the sheet-pan-flat horizon. And yet, inside a gaping industrial dining room downtown, there’s Dougla Kitchen, where diners sip fruity rum drinks out of plastic bags, and acclaimed chef Andrew Black digs deep in his past to bring OKC locals a taste of his Indo-Jamaican upbringing. Don’t miss the Island curry crab and callaloo dip, an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year. — Lesley Suter Los Feliz’s new cocktail bar Vandell, one of Punch’s 2026 Best New Bars, takes over the former Nossa space with a menu of inventive cocktails from industry veterans Shawn Lickliter and Vay Su. Currently, Vandell’s menu features 27 cocktails — 13 original and 14 variations on classics. On the menu, find a handful of takes on a martini, including the Vandell Martini with gin and tarragon vinegar, as well as the Olive Martini with vodka, shio koji, and smoked olive brine. Or, go for one of the market-fresh cocktails named after their main ingredient, like the smoked tomato with mezcal or cucumber with gin. Karla Subero Pittol’s popular dinner party pop-up Chainsaw, a 2026 Best New Bakery, has found a permanent home in Melrose Hill as a pint-sized Venezuelan cafe slinging arepas, pie, and coffee during the daytime. Grab a chair at the interior counter or among the seating splayed out on the sidewalk, and tuck into cafe quesillo, a Venezuelan flan latte, or a Karlita with grapefruit, honey, and tonic. The menu changes often, but constants include arepas stuffed with carne mechada or black beans and white cheese, as well as the famous passionfruit-lime icebox pie with a bracingly tart filling. But the joy of Chainsaw is trying whatever Subero Pittol’s latest creation is, whether that be a hot dog topped with potato sticks on a potato roll or pescadito frito with a whole fried snapper. A tip: gluten-free icebox pie is available in limited quantities — just ask at the register to see if there’s a lucky slice left. — Rebecca Roland Henrietta, a charming all-day deli, market, and restaurant, now lives on the edge of Echo Park and Westlake in the same complex as Clark Street Bakery. During the daytime, Henrietta pairs sandwiches like a broccolini panini and turkey porchetta with deli dishes such as lima bean salad made with Rancho Gordo beans. Evening brings a menu of ricotta dumplings, rigatoni topped with short rib, and a half chicken that’s a nod to San Francisco’s Zuni Cafe. Katie Vonderheide, previously of Silverlake Wine, guides the independent producer-focused wine menu, which spans bottles, including an Old World Chianti, French chilled red, and Spanish cava. The restaurant’s enviable roast chicken is an Eater 2026 Dish of the Year. Perk: Eater members get a free dessert with the purchase of two main dishes through January 31, 2027. Terms apply. After more than six years of development, Washington D.C. restaurateur Rose Previte’s ambitious Maydan Market, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, debuted in early October in West Adams. The hangar-like building houses an outpost of Previte’s D.C. restaurants Compass Rose (which closed earlier this year) and Michelin-recognized Maydan, alongside stalls from five other Los Angeles-based restaurants like Yhing Yhang, Poncho’s Tlayudas, and Tamales Elena. Maydan Market opens with breakfast in the morning from Compass Rose, while the stalls open for lunch; Maydan, the full-service restaurant, is only open for dinner service. Perk: Eater members get a free spread for the table with the purchase of any food item through January 31, 2027. Terms apply. When So. Fox, an Eater 2026 Best New Restaurant, opened in Atlanta’s Virginia-Highland neighborhood in July, chef Myles Moody and sommelier Rachael Pack had an instant hit, bringing new energy to that pocket of the city. The space that formerly housed a burger joint (and before that, an auto repair shop) has been transformed into a bright, perennially packed dining room with grand windows, offering an optimal view of North Highland Avenue. It’s seasonal Southern fare that feels current and relevant, with a refreshingly casual approach. Order the whole roasted chicken; there are only five orders per night. Dishes feature produce from their own Ornewood Park farm, such as the grilled beef with Vidalia onions and braised leeks, and at the end of summer, sugar snap peas with chives and farmer cheese. — Mona Holmes At Ursa, Tucson-based chef Aaron Lopez, an Eater 2026 Chef of the Year, has created a menu imbued with the techniques and flavors of the Sonoran Desert that spans northern Mexico, Arizona, and southeastern California. Inside the high-ceilinged, brick-walled downtown space, Ursa serves as a hushed gallery for Lopez and his team’s $150 tasting menu, which merges Indigenous cooking techniques with foraged and locally farmed ingredients. At every turn, with no extraneous adornments, the kitchen lets the produce and meats boast their innate nature. item.title: Where was The Sound of Music filmed? Retrace the Von Trapps at these filming locations in Salzburg and beyond
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Sound of Music filmed? Despite being over 60 years old, The Sound of Music has endured as one of the most cherished films of all time. Based on a real story, it is set in the picturesque mountainscape of Austria in the 1930s, and follows Maria (Julie Andrews) as she is hired as a governess for the seven children of a widowed man, Captain Georg von Trapp (Christopher Plummer). Featuring some of the most recognisable songs in musical history – including My Favourite Things, Do-Re-Mi, and So Long, Farewell – its charming plot and feel-good premise has captivated audiences for decades. Unsurprisingly, part of the film’s appeal is its setting, which romanticises the tranquillity of being at one with nature. Indeed, it is the subject of one of its most famous songs, The Sound of Music, with much of the action taking place in the bucolic outdoors. Maria’s teaching is inspired by her love of being outside, and this is seen in how she encourages the children to take part in activities including hiking, cross-country skiing and boating. Happily, much of the filming took place on location in Austria itself (where else?). Here’s a guide to where to indulge your inner Von Trapp. Maria spinning around and singing “the hills are alive with the sound of music”, is one of the most iconic scenes in film history. And while The Sound of Music is set in Austria, this scene was actually filmed in… Germany. Specifically, at Mehlweg, a Bavarian mountainscape located six miles from the Salzburg border. Filmmakers settled on this specific location due to its drama, with the Untersberg peak in the background, which gave it that cinematic scope. The exact spot where filming took place is on private land, but you can get pretty close on a Sound of Music tour. One of the other bucolic backdrops in the film is the Gschwandtanger Meadow, which is where Maria and the children have a picnic with the mountains and a castle in the background. It is here that they sing Do-Re-Mi, with Maria accompanying on guitar. The meadow is located in a small town called Werfen, which sits 40 kilometres south of Salzburg, and is known in particular for having the world’s biggest ice cave. The castle, meanwhile, is Hohenwerfen Castle, which was also used as a location in the 1968 Clint Eastwood film, Where Eagles Dare. Unsurprisingly, there is a themed hiking path you can take to the meadow, as well as a specially built set where you can take a photo with Maria and the children. Before Maria is a governess, she wants to become a nun, and the scenes filmed outside her nunnery take place at Nonnberg Abbey in Salzburg. Founded around 714-715 AD, it is the world’s oldest continually existing Benedictine nunnery and was the actual place where the real-life Maria von Trapp was a novice. The Von Trapp family home was largely constructed on a sound stage, but the scenes shot outdoors take place at two locations. One was Schloss Leopoldskron, which was utilised largely for its proximity to a lake. Indeed, the scene in which Maria takes the children boating was filmed here. An 18th-century Rococo palace, today it operates as a hotel, meaning if you want to get a look at the lake, you need to book a stay. Famous guests include King Charles, Arnold Schwarzenegger and Hilary Clinton. The Schloss Frohnburg Palace stood in for the exterior of the Von Trapp family home, with memorable scenes here including when the Captain tears down the flag and the family has to push the car. It was built in the 17th century as a summer house, passed down generations of aristocracy, before being sold to the government and incorporated into the Universität Mozarteum, who use it for student halls, amongst other things. No filming actually took place at Hellbrunn Palace, but it now hosts one of the most famous backdrops of the film. That’s because it has the gazebo – utilised for Sixteen Going On Seventeen and Something Good – in its gardens. The gazebo was actually moved here from Schloss Leopoldskron, where it was originally built for the production, because of the sheer amount of tourists it attracted. It was hoped that by moving its location, it might stand a better chance of being preserved. The doors are kept locked to prevent damage, but you can see it from the outside and take pictures. Various other scenes throughout the film took place in Salzburg Old Town, making it an ideal pitstop if you want to tick off a few locations. The scene in which she sings I Have Confidence en route to her new job as a governess for the Von Trapps shows her walking through Residenzplatz, entering through the Domplatz arches, and splashing in the Residenz Fountain. This is also where the Anschluss scene – Austria’s annexation into Nazi Germany – was also filmed.

item.title: United Airlines 'on track' to debut fancy new regional jet in December
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Who’s ready for first class on United Airlines’s smallest regional jet? The first Mitsubishi CRJ-450, a premium variant of the CRJ-200, is “on track” to begin carrying passengers by the end of the year. That's according to Andrew Nocella, United's chief commercial officer, who discussed the arrival of the CRJ-450 on the sidelines of the brand-new E Concourse at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) on Monday. The plane will debut at the airline’s Chicago O’Hare International Airport (ORD) hub, he added. “It’ll be very exciting and it’s really critical that we connect big cities to little cities, and that’s what the CRJ-450 allows us to do,” said Nocella. Nocella did not say where the CRJ-450 could fly from ORD but it is widely expected to serve some of the smallest cities in United's network, for example Akron-Canton, Ohio, or Fort Wayne, Indiana. United unveiled the CRJ-450 in March in an effort to expand its premium offerings to smaller markets. Instead of the usual 50 economy seats on the CRJ-200, the 450 has seven first-class, 16 extra-legroom economy and 18 economy seats — for a total of 41 — a luggage closet for carry ons and high-speed Starlink inflight WiFi. The CRJ-450 is essentially a premium overhaul to the standard CRJ-200 that has been a workhorse of regional flying for much of this centutry. Passengers have routinely disliked the CRJ-200 for being small and cramped, an experience United hopes to improve with the less-dense CRJ-450 variant. The plane is similar to the CRJ-550, a 50-seat premium variant of the CRJ-700 that typcially seats around 70 passengers. United debuted the CRJ-550 in 2019. The CRJ-450 is the smallest plane in United’s premium airplane menu. Larger offerings include the Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” for premium domestic routes, the A321XLR for long-haul routes and up to the Boeing 787-9s with the “elevated” interior that features the new Polaris Studio in business class. “We have realized that the demand for premium was much higher than we ever knew,” United CEO Scott Kirby, said in March. “It’s like we’re finally creating supply to meet the demand for premium.” United regional affiliate SkyWest Airlines will operate the first 40 CRJ-450s under the United Express brand. The first two CRJ-200s are undergoing the necessary modifications and certification at one of the Utah-based regional carrier’s maintenance facilities, SkyWest President Wade Steel said at the end of October. “The first airplanes just take longer naturally just because you’re working through the first-time issues,” he explained. Subsequent CRJ-200 conversions will take 2 to 3 weeks. Steel, and SkyWest CEO Chip Childs, emphasized that the first CRJ-450s would enter service with United by the end of the year despite at the time having only about eight weeks left in 2026. Both executives were bullish on the opportunity for the CRJ-450. Steel estimated demand for around 100 aircraft in the coming years as major airlines seek to increase premium offerings across their fleets. “Putting first class seats on a CRJ-200 in a very good LOPA [Layout of Passenger Accommodation] with an outstanding interior is a very valuable aircraft,” said Steel Delta Air Lines, for example, joined United in offering the CRJ-550 on regional routes in 2024. SkyWest flies the CRJ-550 for Delta. American Airlines is the only major U.S. carrier not offering the CRJ-550. However, the airline can fly more larger regional jets, particularly the Embraer E175, than either Delta or United under a more lenient contract with its pilots. Related reading:

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Keep Devices Charged While Traveling
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking
A hostel dorm can have many beds but only a few accessible wall outlets. One may be behind a bed frame, and another may already be in use. A compact power strip helps when outlets are scarce, and a power bank covers a different need on days away from the hostel. The ORICO AP3 Travel Power Strip has a 4.1-foot cord that wraps around its body for packing. The cord gives travelers flexibility when the nearest outlet is behind a bed or under a desk. The flat plug takes up less space behind furniture than a plug that sticks straight out from the wall. In a shared room, the layout matters as much as the number of outlets. A strip brings connections within reach, making it easier to plug in a phone and camera battery charger without moving furniture. A nearby shelf or table gives devices a place to sit while charging and keeps the cord out of the walkway. For international trips, travelers should check the exact model's plug type and voltage rating before packing. A plug adapter changes the shape of the connection but leaves the voltage unchanged. It's also worth checking the chargers themselves. Bulky adapters can cover neighboring sockets, so fewer devices may fit than the outlet count suggests. Maps, photos, and restaurant searches drain a phone's battery over a long day. A portable power bank lets travelers recharge between stops, especially when the phone holds a train ticket or directions back to the hostel. The ORICO Pixel Art 10000mAh Power Bank has a rated capacity of 10,000 mAh. That figure is one way to compare power banks. How much charge a phone gains depends on its battery size, energy lost during charging, and whether it's in use while charging. A short, compatible cable kept with the power bank makes it easier to plug in during a lunch break or train ride. A weekend trip with a phone and earbuds may call for a single wall charger and a power bank. A longer trip with a laptop or camera means several devices need charging at the end of the day, so a power strip can be more useful. Checking which devices can share a charger or cable before departure can save space. The power bank and its cable can then stay in an easy-to-reach pocket, ready for the days when an outlet is hard to find. This story was published in partnership with ORICO.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Sausage Stuffing Recipe
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This sausage stuffing has everything you want on your Thanksgiving plate: crisp, craggy edges, a plush, savory center, and plenty of browned sausage throughout. Torn pieces of country-style bread soak up the broth and eggs without falling apart, turning golden and crunchy on top while staying tender underneath. Breakfast sausage does much of the heavy lifting. Once browned, its drippings join plenty of butter to cook the onions, celery, and garlic. Fresh sage, parsley, and thyme bring balance, while optional fennel seeds add a little extra aromatic punch. What kind of sausage should I use? Uncooked pork breakfast sausage is the first choice. Typically seasoned with sage and black pepper, it brings familiar Thanksgiving flavors and plenty of richness. For some heat, choose spicy breakfast sausage. If you can't find the packaged kind or want to avoid pork, try making your own with our breakfast sausage recipe, using ground dark-meat turkey in place of pork. Can I leave the sausage out? This stuffing relies on the fat from breakfast sausage for its flavor. Want a vegetarian version? Our Simple-Is-Best Stuffing is a long-standing reader favorite and was the inspiration for this version; use that recipe with vegetable broth for a meat-free stuffing. What’s the best bread for sausage stuffing? Look for a sturdy country-style white loaf or sourdough with a relatively thin crust. Avoid soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy, and very crusty artisan loaves, which won’t absorb the broth as readily. Even if your bread is a day or two old, don’t skip drying it in the oven—that’s what helps the stuffing hold its shape. Can I make sausage stuffing ahead of time? You can dry the bread a day ahead and store it loosely covered at room temperature. For more ways to get ahead of Thanksgiving, including cooking, refrigerating, and reheating stuffing, see our make-ahead stuffing guide. - Heavy-Duty Aluminum Foil $12 At Target - Made In 9-x-13-inch Baking Dish $89 $40 At Made In Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Grease a 13x9" baking dish with unsalted butter. Arrange one 1–1¼-lb. loaf country-style white bread, torn into 1" pieces, in a single layer on a large rimmed baking sheet and bake until dried out and golden around the edges, 30–40 minutes. Let cool. Step 2Meanwhile, melt 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high heat. Cook 1 lb. breakfast sausage, casings removed if needed, stirring and breaking into small pieces, until well browned and cooked through, 8–10 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer sausage to a small plate, leaving fat behind. Step 3Reduce dial to medium heat and add remaining 8 Tbsp. unsalted butter to fat in pot; heat until melted. Cook 2 medium onions, finely chopped, 6 celery stalks, finely chopped, 8 garlic cloves, coarsely chopped, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. fennel seeds (if using), stirring occasionally, until onions are softened and golden around the edges, 12–15 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 2 cups low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth along with sausage, ½ cup (packed) coarsely chopped parsley, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped sage, 2 Tbsp. finely chopped thyme, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper. Step 4Whisk 3 large eggs and remaining 1 cup low-sodium chicken broth or vegetable broth in a small bowl to combine, then stir into pot (don’t worry, eggs won’t scramble). Add bread to pot and toss gently to combine. Let sit, tossing occasionally, until liquid is almost completely absorbed, about 10 minutes. Step 5Transfer stuffing to prepared dish (don’t pack or press down) and cover loosely with foil. Place dish on a clean large rimmed baking sheet and bake until stuffing is hot throughout (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 160°), 35–45 minutes. Increase oven temperature to 400° and remove foil (no need to remove stuffing from oven while heat increases). Continue to bake until stuffing is light golden brown on top, 25–30 minutes longer. Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 1 day ahead; store loosely covered at room temperature. Stuffing can be assembled 1 day ahead; cover and chill. Bring to room temperature before baking. Editor’s note: This sausage stuffing recipe was first printed in our November 2023 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite Thanksgiving side dishes →

item.title: B.C. Hikers Were Killed in a Rare Predatory Grizzly Attack, Wildlife Officials Say
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Wildlife officials in British Columbia said on Tuesday that they had caught and euthanized the grizzlies involved in a fatal attack on two hikers near Bella Coola earlier this month. In a press conference , B.C. Conservation Officer Service Inspector Jeff Tyre said that DNA testing had “conclusively linked” the female bear and her three cubs to the deaths of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and Selah Reed, 20, the mother and daughter who died in the incident “[The bears] all had to be destroyed, because bears that are involved in fatal attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated,” Tyre said. “This type of behavior presents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.” Notably, Tyre said that forensic evidence from the scene of the attacks led authorities to believe that the bears’ attack on Balcarras and Reed had been predatory, rather than defensive. Such attacks are unusual: A 2019 analysis of brown bear attacks in North America, Europe, and Asia found that only about 5 percent were primarily predatory in nature. In contrast, 47 percent began after the victims encountered a female bear with cubs, 20 percent after a sudden encounter, and 17 percent began due to the presence of a dog. Tyre called the behavior “very rare.” Balcarras and Reed had gone on a hike near their home on October 31. When they had not returned home the next morning, family members reported them missing. Search personnel found Balcarras deceased on November 2, and Reed the following day, both of them with injuries consistent with a bear attack. According to a GoFundMe page established to provide for Balcarras and Reed’s funeral expenses, Balcarras, an art therapist, had only recently moved to Bella Coola. An obituary for Balcarras called her “a gracious, warm-hearted woman” who “believed in accepting people without judgement and showing kindness to everyone who crossed her path. Reed, who worked as an educational assistant, shared her mother’s interest in art, and had recently finished three large murals at Bella Coola’s health center. The tragedy occurred nearly a year after a bear severely injured three children and an adult chaperone who were on a school field trip at a spot just miles away. That bear was never captured, and some observers speculated that the same animal could have been responsible for the deaths. However, Tyre said that the bears that conservation officers had destroyed were not involved in the earlier incident. In the wake of Balcarras’s and Reed’s deaths, the Nuxalk Nation, the Indigenous community in Bella Coola, began to recommend an 8 p.m. curfew to local residents. Samuel Schooner, the Nation’s elected chief councillor, said that the incident had been “deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack.” “We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the timing is right to remove them,” he said. “Our community is rightfully still deeply affected, and will be for generations.”

item.title: Six Feet of Snow Trapped 29 People in the Himalayas. Their Survival Came Down to the Details
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
The mountains around Auden’s Col, an 18,010-foot high-altitude pass in India’s Garhwal Himalayas, looked deceptively calm. It was the afternoon of September 25, 2026; the sky was clear, and the 29-member expedition team had reached base camp at approximately 16,400 feet, preparing to cross one of the region’s most challenging passes the next morning. But within hours, the weather began to change. A fast-moving depression from the Bay of Bengal swept across the Indian subcontinent towards the Himalayas. The Indian government issued a red alert only after the expedition had reached base camp. From the evening of September 25 through September 27, more than six feet of snow fell. “There was no advance warning, and forecasting services failed to predict the severity of the storm,” Vaibhav Kala, the founder of Aquaterra Adventures, the Indian adventure outfitter that organized the expedition, tells Backpacker. “The team was caught in a very rare, heavy weather event.” The group included six clients, three guides, and 20 porters. It was led by Jetendra Singh Rana, a mountaineering guide who had crossed the pass nine times over his 22-year guiding career. Aquaterra Adventures helped open this 10-day route to commercial departures nearly two decades ago. “This is not a casual trek as the route traverses steep slopes, glacier terrain and moraine, to descend onto the heavily crevassed Khatling Glacier,” adds Kala. Rana stepped out of his tent at midnight on the 25th and saw clouds stacking up over the col that hadn’t been there earlier. “Something just did not feel right,” he says. At 2 a.m. on September 26, the sky still hadn’t improved, so he made the first critical decision to call off the next morning’s scheduled ascent to Auden’s Col. By 3:30 a.m., snow had started falling. “No one questioned [Rana’s] decision, and that was the single most important moment during the entire trek that saved our lives,” Preeti and Raj Chauhan, guests from Bangalore, India, say. Had the group left on schedule, they would have been on the face of the col when the snow arrived. By the end of the day, winds had reached around 62 mph, and temperatures had dropped to about -4 degrees Fahrenheit (-20 degrees Celsius). Informed by two decades of guiding experience, Rana’s choice that morning came from a place of pragmatism: “In the mountains, confidence doesn’t mean ignoring danger. It means understanding the situation, trusting your preparation and making responsible decisions,” he says. By the afternoon of September 26, the group’s small sleeping tents were no longer safe because of the snow that continued to fall. At around 4 p.m., Rana moved everyone into a The North Face 2-Meter Dome Tent, which served as the group’s dining tent. Through the night, the wind rose to near-blizzard levels, and the team felt the tent’s metal poles straining. For about two hours, they all took turns pressing on the tent poles from the inside to prevent snow from accumulating. “We are not sure it helped,” Chauhan says. “But it made us feel useful and not panic.” Another guest, Vikram Badhwar, describes a quieter fear. “It is tough to be cooped up in a tent for 48 hours, but no one lost their heads,” he says. “We were joking, laughing, talking and, of course, silently praying for our safe homecoming.” Outside, porters and staff worked through the night with little equipment, shoveling snow off the tent and cutting a perimeter around the base to prevent the rising wall of snow from crushing it. The only communication available to the team was through a satellite phone, which Aquaterra requires all its guides to carry. Rana used it to report the snow and relay his decision to cancel the ascent. By September 26, they were having pre-scheduled status-update calls every few hours. That’s when headquarters concluded that the group could not walk back. Kala called the Uttarakhand tourism secretary, who escalated to the Uttarakhand Disaster Management Authority. The additional district magistrate and divisional forest officer also got involved, along with the Civil Aviation Department and the Indian Army. All six agencies collaborated to requisition nine helicopters to rescue 136 stranded trekkers in the valley, including the Aquaterra team. On the morning of September 27, during an eight-minute phone call, Kala outlined a plan to airlift the entire team. Rana and his staff were instructed to clear a 10-by-10-meter area for a landing pad. The rescue was scheduled for sunrise the following morning. On September 28, the weather cleared for a brief four-hour window. The crew dismantled their safety dome and used the flat surface underneath as a landing pad. Because of the continuing storm, Kala guided the pilots over base camp using Google Earth Imagery from his office in Delhi. The first sortie lifted off about 8:45 a.m. with two passengers. “Departure order was set in advance with the guests so there was no scramble for the aircraft,” says Rana. Aquaterra Adventures was the only group that had given the pilots exact coordinates and a prepared landing zone, keeping them on track. By 11 a.m., all 29 hikers were safe. The first day’s window evacuated 38 people in total from the valley before the weather closed in again. Thankfully, the remaining stranded hikers were evacuated over the next few days with no fatalities. According to Kala and Rana, this rescue was one of the most successful mountain operations in Uttarakhand in recent years, thanks to an unprecedented coordination between state governments, regional municipalities, and private agencies. Kala subsequently submitted a detailed report to the Uttarakhand Government documenting the actions of his team, Rana, and other guides and stakeholders, along with lessons for future expeditions. His key takeaways include focusing on small details like packing a central shelter, shovels, portable power banks, spare satellite-phone charging cables, and ensuring trekkers are always prepared to be rescued. “Our objective was to cross Auden’s Col, but our responsibility was much bigger than reaching a mountain pass,” Rana says. “The mountains will always be there, and there will always be another opportunity to try again. But the safety of every person on an expedition comes first.”

item.title: A Skier Broke Both Legs in an Avalanche, Then Survived More Than 36 Hours in a Crevasse
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Members of France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue team search a snow-covered slope near Pointe Sommeiller in the French Alps after a skier was swept into a crevasse by an avalanche on November 8, 2026. (Photo: CRS Savoie) A backcountry skier in France is lucky to be alive after an avalanche left him trapped in a crevasse for more than 36 hours with both legs broken. The avalanche, which occurred in the French Alps, swept the skier into the crevasse on November 8, according to a Facebook statement from the French national police’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue team. The skier crawled the length of a football field along a passage inside the crevasse, searching for a way out, before rescuers found him alive on November 9. The 39-year-old, whose name has not been released, was on a solo backcountry ski trip near the French-Italian border. He was headed for the summit of Pointe Sommeiller, a 10,932-foot peak known for its steep, technical terrain, according to the French Alpine Club, when the avalanche hit. The peak is located on the France-Italy border, 100 miles east of Grenoble. Details of the rescue were shared in the official Facebook post, and also in a news story published by French newspaper Le Dauphiné Libére. According to these reports, the skier left the Alpine village of Bramans on November 7 and spent the night at a backcountry mountain hut before setting out the following morning to climb Pointe Sommeiller. At the base of a steep, snow-filled chute, he strapped his skis to his pack and began booting up the slope in crampons. His weight triggered a slab avalanche that swept him into a crevasse, fracturing his femur and breaking his other lower leg. Stranded without cell service, he ditched his gear and began crawling down a sloping passage inside the crevasse, hunting for an exit to the surface. He eventually reached a chamber roughly 50 feet beneath the snow, but the slope leading out was too steep to climb with broken legs, Major Yoann Haberey of the CRS Alpes mountain-rescue unit told Le Dauphiné Libéré. A concerned relative reported the skier missing late on November 8, prompting a search that continued until approximately 2 A.M., after the risk of another avalanche forced rescuers to suspend operations. Crews returned the following morning, when a helicopter spotted signs of the avalanche. Search teams began probing and digging through the snow, gradually uncovering the man’s skis and backpack. After more than five hours of excavation, rescuers finally heard his voice coming from roughly 50 feet beneath them. The man was conscious but suffering from hypothermia when crews reached him. They extracted him using a stretcher and winch system, lowered him roughly 650 vertical feet down the mountain, and evacuated him by helicopter to a hospital in southeastern France. The operation involved 22 officers from France’s CRS mountain-rescue unit, six military police rescuers, and three helicopters. “He really is a miracle survivor,” Haberey told Le Dauphiné Libéré. “They were forecasting snowfall overnight, so after that, we weren’t going to go back.” Following the rescue, the CRS Savoie mountain-rescue team urged people heading into the mountains to adjust their plans to current conditions, prepare their routes and equipment, and know when to turn back. “The mountain will always be there tomorrow,” the rescuers wrote.

item.title: These Will Be the Snowiest Adventure Towns This Winter, According to a Meteorologist
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Every year, America’s snowiest towns are typically located in the mountains or on the banks of the Great Lakes. With a few ski resorts already open, if you’re a powder chaser you are likely chomping at the bit for ski season to get into full swing—especially with projections of Super El Niño turbocharging snowfall. I’m a television meteorologist with over 30 years of forecasting experience, as well as an avid skier and snowshoer. Growing up in Greenville, South Carolina, I prayed for snow days. Now, as an adventurer, I chase the powder. A prime sign of Super El Niño’s influence is what just happened in Chile. In late August, a resort called Ski Portillo got multiple snow dumps tallying over 30 inches in a few days. Its record-breaking season hit almost 500 inches, double the typical average. As Super El Niño continues to strengthen, the NOAA Climate Prediction Center is still forecasting a greater-than-83-percent chance of a strong-to-very strong El Niño, likely from January through March. But not everywhere is going to get a stellar snow season. With the strengthened subtropical jet stream, Super El Niño means an active southern storm track and wetter-than-normal conditions for the southern tier of the United States. That favors the Southwest, the Southern Rockies, and California’s Sierra Nevada. The kicker to the season—one that’s not getting a lot of buzz—is the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO), a fluctuation of ocean temperature in the Pacific, entering a cooling phase. That was a big factor in Juneau, Alaska, getting its record-setting snowfall of 201.2 inches during the 2006-7 winter. A strong El Niño and a cool PDO are a highly unusual pairing we haven’t seen since 1972-73, a winter with a significant snowstorm that buried parts of the Southeastern U.S. Then there is the recent weird behavior of the polar vortex, a rotating mass of cold air and low pressure. Its unusual weakening would normally send a significant Arctic blast into the United States, but there’s not enough cold air across Canada yet for this to happen. Simply put, it looks like we’re in for supersized and wild weather this winter. These are my picks for the adventure towns most likely to receive the snowiest winter, including a couple of spots that don’t normally top the “most snow” list. Based on historical records during very strong or Super El Niños, and its maritime air pipeline at full throttle, Mammoth Mountain Ski Area is pretty much a lock for a big snow year. While the 2015-2016 very strong El Niño recorded a near-average season of 393 inches, the 1982-1983 Super El Niño produced a whopping 546.3 inches. In 1983, January picked up 118 inches of snow and March had 112 inches, extending Mammoth’s ski season through late July. Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Take a thrilling ride on the mountain coaster or go snow tubing at Woolly’s Adventure Summit. You can zipline year-round too, or zoom through scenic terrain with Snowmobile Adventures. For a surreal, scenic stop, head to Mono Lake, just 30 minutes away, to see its pogonip ice fog. Because of the lake’s high salinity, it doesn’t freeze. The low-lying ice fog against the limestone tufa towers is otherworldly. Plus, it’s a prime place for wintering waterfowl, such as bald eagles. Basecamp: The Village Lodge Mammoth puts you in the heart of The Village, whereas the historic Mammoth Mountain Inn is best for ski-in/ski-out access. Where to après: For a next-level après, book the VIP Après Experience at Lincoln Bar at Canyon Lodge. For late-night shenanigans, join the “Night Shift” party at Outbound’s Bar Sierra. The best place to chill on a slopeside sundeck is Yodler Restaurant & Bar. For local sips, stop by Shelter Distilling, Mammoth Brewing Company, or Distant Brewing. Yes, there’s skiing in Arizona, and it’s not far from the Grand Canyon. For a high-desert ski experience, the historic settlement of Fort Valley makes the perfect playground for the Arizona Snowbowl. This tiny unincorporated community is just northwest of Flagstaff, which averages more snow annually than Denver or Salt Lake City. With a front-row seat to atmospheric river impulses riding the subtropical jet, Fort Valley and Arizona Snowbowl should have well-above-normal snow totals, with the heaviest snow likely in February. Located in the San Francisco Peaks, Snowbowl historically gets spikes in snowfall during strong El Niño years. During the 2023-24 El Niño, Arizona Snowbowl recorded 281 inches of snow. Its six inches of snow October 24-25, 2026, is a good sign for Arizona’s only ski resort, and for Fort Valley. It is also interesting to note that during the 1972-73 winter of strong El Niño and cool PDO, nearby Flagstaff got a record-setting 210 inches of snow. Off-Slopes Snow Fun: After a morning on the slopes, make a stop at the Museum of Northern Arizona. Don’t miss the “Native Peoples of the Colorado Plateau” and “Southwestern Jewelry” exhibits. Go cross-country skiing or snowshoeing at Arizona Nordic Village or the Peak View Winter Recreation and Parking Area in the Coconino National Forest. Just 20 minutes away, Flagstaff Snow Park is perfect for snow tubing and sledding fun. Take a day trip to Grand Canyon National Park. The South Rim is just over an hour away. The bonus of a winter visit is the lack of crowds. You can easily visit three national monuments in a day: see Ancestral Puebloan dwellings in Walnut Canyon and Wupatki, and experience a moon-like landscape at Sunset Crater Volcano, where every astronaut who has stepped foot on the moon has trained. Bundle up for stargazing at nearby Lowell Observatory in Flagstaff for a truly out-of-this-world evening. Basecamp: Book a mountain cabin for a cozy stay. Basecamp at Snowbowl is a good budget-friendly and pet-friendly option. Plus, you get two complimentary lift tickets per night. Where to après: Basecamp Restaurant is the go-to spot, as it’s less than 5 minutes from Fort Valley and on-site at Basecamp at Snowbowl, located 7 miles from the ski area. You’re also close enough to Flagstaff to devour delicious eats at favorites like Diablo Burger, The Toasted Owl Cafe, or MartAnne’s Burrito Palace. Sitting at 9,800 feet in Dixie National Forest, Brian Head is the highest incorporated town in Utah. The rustic mountain town is named for nearby Brian Head Peak. Dubbed the “highest resort town in America,” it’s home to the small ski area of Brian Head Resort, which has the highest base elevation in Utah. Brian Head is in a sweet spot for Super El Niño’s elevated snow amounts. Plus, its high elevation helps sustain snow quality. Multiple rounds of significant snow in October were the prelude to what should be above-average snowfall and cooler temperatures this winter. Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Soak in the scenery of red rock hoodoos dusted with snow at nearby Cedar Breaks National Monument, where you can go cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. Explore the backcountry on a snowmobile tour with Thunder Mountain Motorsports. Zoom down the hill while snow tubing at Giant Steps Snow Tubing Park. Bundle up to admire the night sky while enjoying a some high-altitude stargazing. Brian Head also makes a great high-elevation base camp for day trips to Bryce Canyon National Park and Zion National Park. Basecamp: Book two nights at Brian Head Lodge and get two free lift tickets with promo code FreedomToSki. There are also numerous cabins and condominiums for rent. Where to après: Last Chair Grill and Brews on the third floor of Giant Steps Lodge is the premier slopeside spot. They boast the largest beer selection in southern Utah and have live music on Fridays and Saturdays. For more low-key options in town, head to 1st Chair Thai and Ramen or Pizanos Pizza. Colorado’s San Juan Mountains are heavily favored for atmospheric rivers to create stellar snow totals. If you want to experience the Alps without leaving the U.S., the San Juans deliver, with their jagged peaks resembling their European counterparts. Telluride is my number-one pick for where I want to go this winter. I love the Victorian architecture in the historic mining town paired with the ski resort experience in Mountain Village, connected by the free Telluride Gondola. Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Whether you go to Bridal Veil Falls—Colorado’s tallest free-falling waterfall—or hike along locals’ favorite, the Jud Wiebe Trail, winter hiking and snowshoeing around Telluride are breathtakingly beautiful. Experience some of the best ice climbing in the world on a guided climb with San Juan Outdoor Adventures. For the ultimate backcountry experience, try heli-skiing or riding with Telluride Helitrax. Go with Telluride Outfitters on a snowmobile tour to Alta Ghost Town—a unique way to experience Telluride’s mining history. Basecamp: I prefer staying in town with the European chalet vibes of The Hotel Telluride being my personal favorite. If your preference is closer to the slopes, the Madeline Hotel and Residences in Mountain Village is excellent. Where to après: Bellying up to the Historic Bar at the New Sheridan Hotel is an absolute must in Telluride. Dating back to 1895, it’s considered one of the most famous bars in the West. Grab pizza at Brown Dog and Pad Thai at Siam. The Butcher and The Baker is always good. On the mountain, sitting outside at Bon Vivant is delightful on a sunny day, and Alpino Vino is the highest fine-dining restaurant in North America. For the best sunset, take the gondola to Allred’s Restaurant. Torrential downpours across the Four Corners caused devastating flooding across Southwestern Colorado. The heavy rains are likely an indicator of deep snowfall to come later in the fall. Historically Wolf Creek gets the most snow in Colorado, with multi-day storms that drop feet of snow, such as the February 17-21, 2026, such as storm cycles that dumped almost five feet of snow (59 inches). During the El Niño winter of 1978-79, Wolf Creek got 807 inches of snow, which is Colorado’s record for a single-season total at a ski area or resort. There are three reasons Wolf Creek gets so much snow. First is its high elevation. The base sits at 10,300 feet. Second is the funneling effect of its local topography. Located just south of the summit of Wolf Creek Pass, it sits in a unique L-shaped bowl that acts like a catchall basin for snow. Third are the storm tracks pushing up against the San Juans, which should bode well for a high snow total this season. Off-Slopes Snow Fun: As one of the premier destinations on Colorado’s 800-mile Historic Hot Springs Loop, Pagosa Springs on the west side of Wolf Creek Pass is perfect for a ski-and-soak getaway. Hike to frozen Treasure Falls. The 105-foot plunge waterfall between Wolf Creek Ski Area and Pagosa Springs freezes into massive ice columns, attracting technical ice climbers. Take the scenic drive, then hike the Piedra Ice Fissures Trail to see ice caves. Satisfy your need for speed by snowmobiling in the San Juan National Forest and to the Continental Divide on a guided tour with Wolf Creek Snowmobile Tours. You can also take a day trip to see the cliff dwellings in Mesa Verde National Park. Basecamp: There is no lodging at the ski area, so plan to stay in Pagosa Springs. My favorite is The Springs Resort and Spa. It’s home to the Mother Spring, the deepest geothermal hot spring in the world, certified at a depth of at least 1,002 feet by Guinness World Records. If you stay there, you get 24-hour access to the soaking pools. The Clouds in My Coffee pool is my favorite for an early morning soak with coffee in hand. If you don’t want to drive and park in one of the free on-mountain lots, Wilderness Journeys Pagosa runs a daily shuttle, but you need to make a reservation in advance. Where to après: Sip an IPA at Riff Raff Brewing Company. Savor a craft cocktail at The Neon Mallard. Order the fish tacos at Kip’s Grill. You’ll thank me later. Relax with a latte or tea at the Root House. The founders of this cool coffeehouse and shop are the stars in HGTV’s Building Roots. The cinnamon rolls are sinfully good. Finally, grab a sandwich or quiche at Pagosa Baking Company. Famous for its historic adobe architecture and vibrant art scene, Taos doesn’t normally rank high on the list of America’s snowiest adventure towns. But this year it could, since it’s in the favorable storm track of the active subtropical jet stream. Less than 20 miles north of town, Taos Ski Valley has over 300 inches of snow annually. In town, snow typically peaks in December and January but continues to fall well into March at the ski resort. Angel Fire Resort is also about 45 minutes away. Off-Slopes Snow Fun: Taos Pueblo is a UNESCO World Heritage Site that’s been inhabited for over 1,000 years. With the chill in the air and fireplaces glowing, I love visiting the pueblo in December. Grab a latte in Dawn Butterfly then stroll through the artisan shops, such as Pueblo Runner. Make sure to sample the fry bread while visiting. Taos Pueblo does close annually for six to eight weeks in late winter and early spring for traditional ceremonies. Beyond the nearby slopes, you can also go snowshoeing, cross-country skiing, or winter hiking in the Carson National Forest. Soak in the therapeutic waters at Ojo Caliente, about an hour away from Taos. There are several museums and historic homes to tour in town, or you can simply stroll around Taos Plaza. The historic district is filled with art galleries and unique boutiques. Chocolate + Cashmere is my favorite spot to find something cozy, and the Sage Fine Art Gallery is filled with works by award-winning local artists. Basecamp: If you want to stay where you ski or ride, The Blake is a ski-in/ski-out property at Taos Ski Valley. Just outside of the town’s busy historic district, Hotel Willa is an delightful option for an upscale boutique stay with character in a remodeled 1960s adobe motor lodge. For something completely off-grid, book a stay at Earthship Biotecture. Where to après: The Bavarian is a fun option at the base of Taos Ski Valley. It’s famous for its German eats and draft beer. In town, the Adobe Bar is a classic après haunt next to historic Doc Martin’s Restaurant. My favorite place in town to chow down is Orlando’s New Mexican Café. Go hungry, and order the blue corn enchiladas. New Mexican enchiladas are layered, rather than rolled. Located on the cusp of the transition zone between wet and dry, historical data shows mixed results for the northern Sierra. Strong El Niños trend toward below-normal seasons, while very strong El Niños historically produce above-normal snow averages. It’s a roll of the dice for Tahoe. Strong El Niños typically mean warmer-than-average winter temperatures for Washington State, but Super El Niños add ample moisture-laden Pacific air that could mean localized wet storms. Glacier is the closest town to Mount Baker Ski Area, which holds the world record for the most snowfall in a single season of 1,140 inches in 1998-99 season [cut]. That was during a strong La Niña season, but I’m never ruling out Mount Baker for big snow totals. In past Super El Niño winters, Mount Baker Ski Area still recorded an average of 642 inches of snow. Thanks to intense lake-effect snow off Lake Ontario, Redfield often tops the list of the snowiest places in the Great Lakes with 380-plus inches of snow annually. This winter looks milder and drier for the Great Lakes. But record-warm lake temperatures on the Great Lakes mean heavy lake-effect snow could pile up quickly when cold Arctic air arrives. Intense, localized lake-effect snow squalls look more likely this winter across the Great Lakes. With the NOAA Winter Outlook showing warmer-than-normal and wetter conditions, there’s the potential for heavy, wet snow events. Another key factor is that powerful coastal nor’easters occasionally develop during historical super El Niños. Typical timing for those is late January through February. While not normally one of America’s snowiest towns, the powerful subtropical jet stream pulling moisture from the Gulf of Mexico significantly increases precipitation across the Southeast. If a cold-air damming wedge sets up with ample moisture, that means a major winter storm in the Blue Ridge Mountains. The February 1973 “Great Southeastern Snowstorm” is proof that the Deep South sometimes measures snow in feet instead of only an inch or two.
